name: Modular Exponentiation a^b mod n
description: Computes a^b mod n exactly by repeated squaring, without ever forming the huge power a^b — the core operation of RSA and Diffie–Hellman.
notes: Exact for any size of a and b (n up to about 9 × 10^15). 7^40 mod 13 = 9. A negative exponent uses the modular inverse of a. RSA encrypts with c = m^e mod n and decrypts with m = c^d mod n.

name: Modular Inverse
description: Finds x with a·x ≡ 1 (mod m), which exists exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1.
notes: modinv(17, 3120) = 2753: the private exponent in the classic RSA example with p = 61, q = 53, e = 17.

name: Modular Division a/b mod m
description: Divides a by b modulo m by multiplying with the inverse of b (requires gcd(b, m) = 1).

name: Least Non-negative Residue
description: Reduces a modulo m to the range 0 … m − 1, also for negative a (the mathematician's mod).
notes: −17 ≡ 3 (mod 5). The plain % operator keeps the sign of a and would give −2.

name: Congruence Test a ≡ b (mod m)
description: Returns 1 when m divides a − b, i.e. a and b leave the same remainder modulo m.
notes: 38 ≡ 14 (mod 12): on a clock, 38 hours after midnight shows the same time as 14 hours after.

name: Linear Congruence ax ≡ b (mod m): Smallest Solution
expression: if(mod(b, gcd(a, m)) != 0, -1, mod(b / gcd(a, m) * if(m / gcd(a, m) == 1, 0, modinv(a / gcd(a, m), m / gcd(a, m))), m / gcd(a, m)))
description: Solves a·x ≡ b (mod m). A solution exists when g = gcd(a, m) divides b; the solutions are x₀ + k·m/g, and this returns the smallest x₀ ≥ 0 (or −1 if there is none).
notes: 14x ≡ 30 (mod 100) has g = 2 and the solutions 45, 95.

name: Number of Solutions of ax ≡ b (mod m)
description: Counts the solutions modulo m of the linear congruence a·x ≡ b: gcd(a, m) of them when gcd(a, m) divides b, otherwise none.
notes: 14x ≡ 30 (mod 100) has exactly 2 solutions modulo 100.

name: Chinese Remainder Theorem (Two Congruences)
description: Finds the smallest x ≥ 0 with x ≡ a₁ (mod m₁) and x ≡ a₂ (mod m₂). With coprime moduli the answer is unique modulo m₁m₂.
notes: Non-coprime moduli also work when the congruences agree; otherwise the result is empty. Here x = 8.

name: Chinese Remainder Theorem (Three Congruences)
expression: crt(a1, m1, a2, m2, a3, m3)
description: Solves three simultaneous congruences x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ), returning the smallest non-negative solution.
notes: Sunzi's original puzzle (remainders 2, 3, 2 for 3, 5, 7) has the answer 23.

name: Fermat's Little Theorem Check
description: Computes a^(p−1) mod p, which equals 1 for every prime p not dividing a (Fermat's little theorem).
notes: A result other than 1 proves that p is composite.

name: Euler's Theorem Check
description: Computes a^φ(n) mod n, which equals 1 whenever gcd(a, n) = 1 (Euler's theorem, generalising Fermat's little theorem).
notes: Reduces huge exponents: a^k ≡ a^(k mod φ(n)) (mod n) for a coprime to n.

name: Last Digits of a Power
description: Gives the last d decimal digits of a^b without computing the whole power.
notes: 2^1000 ends in …069376; the leading zero of the ending is not shown, so the result reads 69376.

name: Multiplicative Order ord_n(a)
description: Gives the smallest k ≥ 1 with a^k ≡ 1 (mod n); requires gcd(a, n) = 1.
notes: ord₇(10) = 6, which is why 1/7 = 0.142857… repeats with period 6.

name: Smallest Primitive Root
description: Gives the smallest g whose powers run through every residue coprime to n. Primitive roots exist only for n = 1, 2, 4, p^k and 2p^k.
notes: The smallest primitive root of 41 is 6.

name: Primitive Root Test
description: Returns 1 when g is a primitive root modulo n, i.e. its order equals φ(n).
notes: 3 is a primitive root of 17 (and so of every Fermat prime above 3).

name: Number of Primitive Roots
description: Counts the primitive roots modulo n (when any exist): φ(φ(n)).
notes: There are φ(40) = 16 primitive roots modulo 41.

name: Discrete Logarithm (Brute Force)
expression: sum(k, 0, p - 2, k * (powmod(g, k, p) == h))
description: Finds the exponent k with g^k ≡ h (mod p), where g is a primitive root modulo the prime p, by trying every k.
notes: Here 3^4 = 81 ≡ 13 (mod 17), so k = 4. Only practical for p up to about a million; its difficulty for large p secures Diffie–Hellman.

name: Legendre Symbol (a/p)
description: Gives 1 if a is a nonzero square modulo the odd prime p, −1 if it is not, and 0 if p divides a.

name: Jacobi Symbol (a/n)
description: Extends the Legendre symbol to any odd n > 0 as the product of Legendre symbols over the prime factors of n.
notes: Computed quickly by quadratic reciprocity without factoring. A value of −1 proves a is a non-residue; +1 does not prove it is a residue.

name: Kronecker Symbol (a/2)
description: Gives the Kronecker symbol (a/2): 0 for even a, +1 when a ≡ ±1 (mod 8) and −1 when a ≡ ±3 (mod 8).
notes: This value also tells whether 2 is a quadratic residue modulo an odd prime (second supplement to quadratic reciprocity).

name: Euler's Criterion
description: Computes a^((p−1)/2) mod p, which is 1 when a is a quadratic residue modulo p and p − 1 when it is not.
notes: For p = 11 and a = 5 the result is 1, so 5 is a square modulo 11.

name: Quadratic Residue Test
description: Returns 1 when x² ≡ a (mod n) has a solution, checking every x (works for any modulus, prime or not).
notes: 10 ≡ 6² (mod 13). Loops over n values, so keep n modest.

name: Modular Square Root (p ≡ 3 mod 4)
description: For a prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and a quadratic residue a, returns a square root of a modulo p as a^((p+1)/4).
notes: The other root is p minus this one. 2 ≡ 4² ≡ 3² (mod 7); the formula gives 4.

name: Number of Quadratic Residues mod p
description: Exactly half of the nonzero residues modulo an odd prime are squares.
notes: Modulo 101 there are 50 quadratic residues and 50 non-residues.

name: Sum of Legendre Symbols over a Range
description: Adds (a/p) for a from 1 to n: the excess of residues over non-residues among the first n numbers.
notes: The Pólya–Vinogradov inequality bounds such character sums by √p ln p.

name: Period of the Decimal Expansion of 1/n
description: Gives the length of the repeating block of 1/n in decimal: the order of 10 modulo n with its factors 2 and 5 removed.
notes: 1/7 = 0.(142857) has period 6; 1/12 = 0.08(3) has period 1. Terminating decimals give 1.

name: Pre-period of the Decimal Expansion of 1/n
description: Gives the number of decimal digits of 1/n before the repeating part starts: the larger of the exponents of 2 and 5 in n.
notes: 1/12 = 0.08333… has pre-period 2 (the digits 0 and 8).

name: Full Reptend Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when 1/p has the longest possible decimal period p − 1 (10 is a primitive root modulo p).
notes: 7, 17, 19, 23, 29, 47, … are full reptend primes; 1/7 generates the cyclic number 142857.

name: Cyclic Number from a Full Reptend Prime
description: Builds the cyclic number (10^(p−1) − 1)/p, whose multiples by 1 … p − 1 are rotations of its own digits.

name: Casting Out Nines
description: Gives n mod 9, which equals the repeated digit sum (except that 9 becomes 0). Used for centuries to check arithmetic by hand.
notes: If a × b = c is right, then (a mod 9)(b mod 9) ≡ c (mod 9); a mismatch reveals an error.

name: Divisibility by 11 (Alternating Digit Sum)
description: Computes the alternating sum of the digits of n from the right. n is divisible by 11 exactly when this is divisible by 11.

name: Divisibility by 7 (Remove Last Digit Rule)
description: Removes the last digit and subtracts twice it from the rest. n is divisible by 7 exactly when the result is; repeat until small.

name: RSA Public Modulus and Totient
description: Gives λ(pq) = lcm(p − 1, q − 1), the Carmichael totient used to compute RSA private exponents.
notes: For p = 61, q = 53, λ = 780 (φ = 3120 also works but gives larger exponents).

name: RSA Private Exponent
description: Computes the RSA private exponent d = e⁻¹ mod λ(pq).
notes: With p = 61, q = 53, e = 17 this gives d = 413. Real keys use primes hundreds of digits long.

name: Diffie–Hellman Shared Secret
description: Computes the shared key (g^b)^a mod p that Alice derives from Bob's public value; Bob gets the same number as (g^a)^b.
notes: The classic example with p = 23, g = 5, a = 6, b = 15 gives the secret 2.

name: ElGamal Encryption (Second Component)
description: Computes c₂ = m·h^k mod p, the masked message in ElGamal encryption (c₁ = g^k mod p is sent alongside).
notes: Values follow the Handbook of Applied Cryptography example (p = 2357, g = 2, x = 1751, m = 2035 there).

name: Linear Congruential Generator Step
description: Advances a linear congruential pseudo-random generator: x_{n+1} = (a·x_n + c) mod m.
notes: Defaults are the constants of the classic C library rand(). Full period m needs c coprime to m and a − 1 divisible by every prime factor of m (and by 4 if 4 divides m).

name: Lehmer RNG Step (MINSTD)
description: Advances the Park–Miller "minimal standard" generator x_{n+1} = 48271·x_n mod (2^31 − 1).
notes: The state must be between 1 and 2^31 − 2. C++ std::minstd_rand uses exactly this rule.

name: Blum Blum Shub Step
description: Advances the Blum Blum Shub generator x_{n+1} = x_n² mod pq, a cryptographically secure generator whose output bit is the parity of x.
notes: The worked example with p = 11, q = 23 and seed 3 gives 9, 81, 236, 36 and so on.

name: Modular Arithmetic Clock Addition
description: Gives the hour shown on a 12-hour clock t hours after hour h (0 stands for 12).
notes: 50 hours after 9 o'clock the clock shows 11.

name: Pisano Period π(m) (Brute Force)
expression: sum(k, 1, 6 * m, k * and(mod(fib(k), m) == 0, mod(fib(k + 1), m) == 1) * (sum(j, 1, k - 1, and(mod(fib(j), m) == 0, mod(fib(j + 1), m) == 1)) == 0))
description: Gives the period with which the Fibonacci numbers repeat modulo m, found as the first k with F_k ≡ 0 and F_(k+1) ≡ 1.
notes: The period is at most 6m. Modulo 10 the last digits of Fibonacci numbers repeat every 60 terms. Uses exact Fibonacci numbers, so m should stay below about 12.

name: Wilson Quotient W(p) mod p
description: Gives the Wilson quotient ((p − 1)! + 1)/p reduced modulo p. It is 0 exactly for Wilson primes (5, 13, 563).

name: Fermat Quotient q_p(a)
description: Gives the Fermat quotient (a^(p−1) − 1)/p reduced modulo p. It is 0 exactly when p is a Wieferich prime to base a.

name: Number of Square Roots of a mod p
description: Counts the solutions of x² ≡ a (mod p): 2 for a quadratic residue, 0 for a non-residue, 1 when p divides a.
notes: 2 has two square roots modulo 7 (3 and 4).

name: Square Roots of 1 mod n
description: Counts the x between 1 and n with x² ≡ 1 (mod n).
notes: Modulo 24 every odd number coprime to 24 works: 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 — eight of them.

name: Period of the Binary Expansion of 1/p
description: Gives the length of the repeating block of 1/p in binary: the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p.
notes: 1/11 in binary repeats every 10 bits.

name: Cyclotomic Polynomial Value Φ_n(x)
description: Evaluates the n-th cyclotomic polynomial at x with the Möbius formula Φ_n(x) = ∏_{d|n} (x^d − 1)^μ(n/d).
notes: Φ₁₂(x) = x⁴ − x² + 1, so Φ₁₂(2) = 13. Primes dividing Φ_n(a) are ≡ 1 (mod n) or divide n.

name: Integers up to x Coprime to n
expression: sum(d, 1, n, if(mod(n, d) == 0, mu(d) * floor(x / d), 0))
description: Counts the integers from 1 to x that share no factor with n, by inclusion–exclusion over the divisors of n.
notes: Up to 100 there are 26 numbers coprime to 30.

name: Value of Digits in Base b
expression: sum(k, 1, len(v), at(v, k) * b^(len(v) - k))
description: Converts a list of base-b digits (most significant first) to an ordinary number.
notes: 1011 in binary is 11. Hexadecimal digits A–F are entered as 10–15.

name: Writing n in Base b (Digits Shown as a Number)
expression: sum(k, 0, floor(logb(n, b) + 1e-9), mod(floor(n / b^k), b) * 10^k)
description: Shows n in base b by reading the base-b digits as a decimal numeral (for bases up to 10).
notes: 11 becomes 1011 in binary and 13 in octal.
